lesson.title: Behind the Curtain: How a Mechanism Explains a Rate Law
lesson.summary: A reaction mechanism is the proposed step-by-step molecular pathway from reactants to products, and its slowest elementary step controls the overall rate, which is why a real rate law so often looks nothing like the balanced equation would suggest.
lesson.body:
A reaction mechanism is a sequence of elementary steps that, taken together, describes how a reaction actually happens at the molecular level. A valid mechanism has to satisfy two hard requirements. First, when you add up all the elementary steps, everything has to cancel and combine to reproduce the overall balanced equation exactly, nothing more and nothing less. Second, the rate law predicted by the mechanism has to match the rate law actually measured in the lab (using the method of initial rates you will revisit in the next chapter). A mechanism that fails either test gets rejected or revised; a mechanism that passes both is not proven true in some absolute sense, but it becomes a strongly supported hypothesis for what is really going on.

Species that appear in one step as a product and then get consumed in a later step are called intermediates. They are real chemical species, they genuinely exist for a short time, but they do not appear anywhere in the overall balanced equation, because they get produced and used up entirely within the sequence of steps.

When a mechanism has more than one step, those steps almost never proceed at the same speed. One step is typically much slower than the others, and that slow step acts like a bottleneck: no matter how fast the other steps are, the reaction as a whole cannot go any faster than its slowest step allows. Chemists call this the rate-determining step (RDS), and because it is (by definition) an elementary step, you can write its rate law directly from its own coefficients, exactly as shown in the Elementary Steps chapter. That rate law, from the slow step alone, is the predicted overall rate law for the whole mechanism.

Here is a classic worked example: the overall reaction NO2(g) + CO(g) -> NO(g) + CO2(g). If you tried to guess its rate law from the balanced equation, you would expect something like rate = k[NO2][CO], first order in each reactant. But this reaction is commonly explained by a two-step mechanism:

Step 1 (slow): NO2 + NO2 -> NO3 + NO
Step 2 (fast): NO3 + CO -> NO2 + CO2

Check first that these two steps really do add up to the overall equation. Adding the left sides and right sides of both steps gives:

NO2 + NO2 + NO3 + CO -> NO3 + NO + NO2 + CO2

NO3 appears on both sides, so it cancels completely, confirming it is a reactive intermediate, not a product. One NO2 on the left cancels against the NO2 on the right, leaving one NO2 on the left. What remains is:

NO2 + CO -> NO + CO2

which is exactly the overall balanced equation. The mechanism passes the first test.

Now derive the predicted rate law from the rate-determining step, step 1, which is elementary and bimolecular (two NO2 molecules colliding):

rate = k1[NO2]^2

Notice this predicted rate law is second order in NO2 and zero order in CO, nothing like the naive k[NO2][CO] guess you would make from the overall balanced equation, and nothing like the coefficients of the overall equation would suggest on their own. This is the entire point of studying mechanisms: the overall equation only tells you where you start and where you end up, not the path in between, and it is the slow step of that path, not the overall stoichiometry, that determines the rate law. If experiments on this reaction genuinely show a rate law of k[NO2]^2, that measurement is strong support for this two-step mechanism; if instead experiments showed a different order, this proposed mechanism would need to be revised or abandoned in favor of one whose slow step matches the data.
